descriptions.TNiE3F-dBu8:
The Krishnamurti Podcast - Ep. 306 - Krishnamurti on Totality

‘When we understand the totality, the whole picture of life, our particular issues and problems are resolved.’

This episode on Totality has four sections.

The first extract (2:38) is from the first discussion at Brockwood Park in 1976, and is titled: Seeing the Totality of One’s Life.

The second extract (9:59) is from Krishnamurti’s first talk in Saanen 1965, and is titled: Unless We See the Totality of Existence, There Is No Way Out.

The third extract (41:34) is from the third talk in Madras 1967, and is titled: Awareness of Totality.

The final extract in this episode (1:01:32:) is from Krishnamurti’s ninth talk in Paris 1961, and is titled: Total Stillness of the Mind.

The Krishnamurti Podcast features carefully selected extracts from his talks. Each episode highlights Krishnamurti’s different approaches to universal and timeless themes relevant to everyday life, the state of the world and the future of humanity. This episode’s theme is Totality. Upcoming themes are Logic and Reason, The Unknown, and Laziness and Inertia.

This is a podcast from Krishnamurti Foundation Trust, based at Brockwood Park in the UK, which is also home to the Krishnamurti Retreat Centre. Situated in the beautiful countryside of the South Downs National Park, The Krishnamurti Centre offers retreats individually and in groups. The focus is on inquiry in light of Krishnamurti’s teachings in a conducive atmosphere. Please visit krishnamurticentre.org.uk for more information, including our volunteer programme.

You can also find our regular Krishnamurti quotes and videos on social media at Krishnamurti Foundation Trust.

descriptions.LZ4se_3eqo0:
Urgency of Change - The Krishnamurti Podcast - Ep. 305 - Krishnamurti on Non-violence

‘I am violent. I project an idea of non-violence, and hope the pursuit of non-violence will help me to be free of violence. In the pursuit of non-violence I am still being violent.’

This episode on Non-violence has four sections.

The first extract (2:36) is from Krishnamurti’s first talk at Rajghat 1963, and is titled: The Fiction of Non-violence

The second extract (14:06) is from the third discussion at Brockwood Park School in 1983, and is titled: The Violent Pursuit of Non-violence.

The third extract (31:51) is from Krishnamurti’s second talk in Ojai 1983, and is titled: Ending Violence Completely.

The final extract in this episode (52:40) is from a direct recording in Ojai 1983, and is titled: Insight Banishes All Violence.

The Krishnamurti Podcast features carefully selected extracts from his public talks. Each episode highlights Krishnamurti’s different approaches to universal and timeless themes relevant to everyday life, the state of the world and the future of humanity. This episode’s theme is Non-violence. Upcoming themes are Totality, Logic and Reason, and The Unknown.

This is a podcast from Krishnamurti Foundation Trust, based at Brockwood Park in Hampshire, UK. Brockwood is also home to Brockwood Park School, a unique international boarding school offering a personalised, holistic education inspired by Krishnamurti’s teachings. Please visit brockwood.org.uk for more information.

You can also find our regular Krishnamurti quotes and videos on social media at Krishnamurti Foundation Trust.

descriptions.jqxFbQ5FBB4:
Krishnamurti Foundation Trust is pleased to share the newly digitised 4K edition of Krishnamurti’s 1966 groundbreaking series 'The Real Revolution'. These eight programmes were originally produced and broadcast in America by the National Educational Television Network. They represent the earliest films of Krishnamurti speaking to audiences – it was the first time he had allowed his talks and discussion groups to be filmed. The complete eight-part series is available to watch for free.
──────────
Subtitles available: Chinese, Dutch, English, Estonian, Finnish, French, German, Greek, Gujarati, Italian, Japanese, Latvian, Malayalam, Norwegian, Polish, Portuguese, Russian, Slovenian, Spanish, Turkish, and Vietnamese
──────────
The End of Conflict — The Real Revolution • Krishnamurti (Ep. 8/8)

Why are we discontented, and with what? Being discontented with what is, we develop the idea of what should be. There is conflict between what is and what should be. 

The centre in consciousness, the observer, creates a space around itself which is always limited. The center is the accumulation of knowledge and experience. There is no freedom in that space.

Can the mind be intensely alert without experience? Such a mind is the religious mind.
──────────

Living and Death — The Real Revolution • Krishnamurti (Ep. 7/8)

To understand the problem of death, one has to be free of fear. Fear is thought in action with regard to the past, through the present and to the future. Fear is the movement of time, which is essentially the process of thinking. How one looks at fear matters immensely.

Death is the ending of all the things which have been accumulated, which is the known. Losing the known means complete loneliness.

Can one die every day to one’s experience? So that every experience is totally assimilated, understood and dissolved. This requires a great deal of energy, which is attention.

© 1966 Krishnamurti Foundation of America and Krishnamurti Foundation Trust

Questioning — The Real Revolution • Krishnamurti (Ep. 6/8) – Krishnamurti with students at the Thacher School

One should have a bit of skepticism when asking questions. A wrong question will have no answer, but a right question, in its very asking, unfolds the understanding of it. It needs intelligence and sensitivity to ask the right question and to see all that is involved in it and go to the very end of it.

What is Love? — The Real Revolution • Krishnamurti (Ep. 5/8)

What is the state of the mind that asks a question? Who is going to answer it? How does one find out what love is? Is love pleasure? Will the conscious mind find it out? If I make a conscious effort then I must have recognition of what it is. 

To enquire, one must be free of belief, and therefore of fear. To find out what love is, one must enquire into the question of pleasure and desire. Thought gives desire continuity and vitality. This must be discovered actually for oneself. Is it possible to look at something extraordinarily beautiful and merely observe, without the interference of thought?

Meditation — The Real Revolution • Krishnamurti (Ep. 4/8)

The world is full of misery and conflict, destructive brutality, aggression. Man has mastered the external world but inwardly he is still violent, acquisitive, competitive. Society has been built along these lines. The crisis in the world is actually a crisis in consciousness. It is important to bring about a revolution in the human mind. 

“What we are trying, in all these discussions and talks here, is to see if we cannot radically bring about a transformation of the mind. Not accept things as they are. Nor revolt against it – revolt doesn’t answer a thing! But to understand it, to go into it, to examine it; give your heart and your mind with everything that you have to find out a way of living differently.”

Freedom From Fear — The Real Revolution • Krishnamurti (Ep. 3/8)

Passion is needed to understand the whole complex problem of existence. This passion cannot be supplied by the intellect or by sentiment or emotionalism, or aroused by committing oneself to a cause.

The psychological structure of society is based on pleasure. Our whole psychological existence is based in the continuation of pleasure. Until one understands the nature and the structure of pleasure, there will always be fear. The mind that is conditioned by the principle of pleasure cannot think clearly. What is pleasure?

Observing Ourselves — The Real Revolution • Krishnamurti (Ep. 2/8)

Man has made himself incapable of facing what is, inwardly. Therefore he has a concept about it and acts according to that concept. Therefore the fact, the concept and action are in contradiction and there is a battle going on. The interval between the observer and the observed is time, containing numerous ideas which prevent actual observation of the fact.

In relationship, the observer is the image, looking at an image which has been created about the other. So the relationship between the observer and the observed is not actually relationship. When the observer has no image, then the observer is not different from observation. ‘What is’ is the observer, not ‘the observer is looking at what is’. There is no quality of choice in this.
